subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Ganymede: The Giant Moon
description: A 60-second lesson on Ganymede: The Giant Moon.

hook.text: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system—bigger than Mercury. It has its own magnetic field.

buildup.text: It's about 5,270 km across. Half its surface is old and cratered; the other half has younger grooved terrain.

discovery.text: Ganymede is the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field—produced by a liquid iron core deep inside.

twist.text: Hubble observations suggest a subsurface ocean sandwiched between layers of ice, perhaps 100 km below the surface.

climax.text: ESA's JUICE mission will orbit Ganymede in the 2030s—the first spacecraft to orbit a moon other than our own.

punchline.text: Bigger than Mercury. Its own magnetic field. An ocean hiding in the deep.

quiz.question: What makes Ganymede unique among all moons in the solar system?
options: It is the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field
It is the only moon larger than a planet
It has the most volcanically active surface of any moon

details.summary: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system — bigger than Mercury and the only moon with its own magnetic field. It likely harbors a subsurface ocean sandwiched between layers of ice.
details.whyItMatters: Ganymede's magnetic field and possible ocean make it scientifically unique. ESA's JUICE mission will study it in detail, potentially revealing whether moons with internal oceans are common in the solar system.
takeaways: Largest moon in the solar system, bigger than Mercury
Only moon with its own intrinsic magnetic field
Likely harbors a deep subsurface ocean

faq.question: How can a moon have its own magnetic field?
faq.answer: Ganymede likely has a liquid iron core that generates a magnetic field through dynamo action, similar to Earth. This makes it unique among moons. The field creates a small magnetosphere within Jupiter's much larger one. How the core stays liquid in a moon this old is an active research question.

faq.question: What will the JUICE mission study at Ganymede?
faq.answer: ESA's JUICE (Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer), launched in 2023, will orbit Ganymede starting in 2034 — the first spacecraft to orbit a moon other than our own. It will study the ocean, magnetic field, surface, and interior using radar, magnetometers, spectrometers, and cameras.
